name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is a hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a masked figure dressed as a Tatar warrior who parades the Old Town on the octave of Corpus Christi, striking onlookers with a wooden mace for luck. The procession commemorates the defeat of a Mongol raid, and the figure has been a beloved Kraków festival emblem for centuries.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Polish tradition, evolved from the konfederatka worn by Bar Confederation troops in 1768 and later the standard Polish military cap. Its four corners mark the four sides of the world, and it remains a national and military symbol worn in parades and folk ensembles.
source: Histories of Polish military dress

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is Polish folk paper-cutting, most famously the colourful layered cutouts of Łowicz, made with sheep shears from dyed paper. Designs show birds, suns, flowers and village scenes, and were pasted on walls and beams to brighten rural homes, particularly in Mazovia and Kurpie regions.
source: Studies of Polish folk paper-cutting

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a colourful Nativity crib built as a miniature of Kraków's architecture, with towers, spires and gilt foil, crafted by krakowianie and judged each December in a contest at the Rynek. The tradition, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018, blends the Nativity scene with civic pride and Christmas carolling.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of willow twigs used on Easter Monday in the Czech lands, when boys lightly switch girls to keep them fresh and healthy, receiving painted eggs in return. Made of eight to twelve woven twigs bound with ribbon, it carries an old spring-renewal meaning in Czech folk custom.
source: Czech and Slovak ethnography of Easter customs

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted glass baubles produced around Jablonec nad Nisou since the mid-19th century. Tiny beads and figurines are strung for the tree, and the region's skilled glassworkers made Christmas ornaments a famous export prized for their delicate silvering and colours.
source: Histories of Bohemian glassmaking

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a long overtone flute of Slovak shepherds, up to two metres long, made from elder or maple wood with a unique air duct. Played while standing, it produces a deep humming bass; its sound and technique were inscribed by UNESCO in 2008 as a living shepherd tradition.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotárstvo, or wire craft, is the Slovak art of reinforcing cracked pottery and glass with fine iron wire, practised by travelling drotár craftsmen from the 18th century. Wire-bound jugs, bottles and bowls became folk masterpieces, and the craft was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnography

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small shepherd's axe of the Carpathian Highlands, a light axe on a long decorated wooden handle used as a staff, tool and weapon by Slovak bača shepherds. Legend credits it as the weapon of Jánošík, and it became a badge of the highland shepherd's life.
material: forged iron blade, carved wood handle
source: Slovak folklore and highland ethnography

name: Bogrács
description: A bogrács is a black cast-iron cauldron hung over an open fire, the essential vessel of Hungarian gulyás and pörkölt cooking. Its three legs and swing-arm let cooks stir the stew over flame, and bogrács gatherings are a central social ritual of Hungarian outdoor cookery.
source: Hungarian culinary and folk ethnography

name: Matyó Embroidery
description: Matyó embroidery is the vivid floral needlework of Mezőkövesd in Hungary, with large rose, tulip and peony motifs in red, blue and green silk on white linen. Worn on festive costumes and home textiles, the technique was inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as a living community craft.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Hungarian textile studies

name: Székely Kapu
description: The Székely kapu is the richly carved wooden gate of the Hungarian Székely villages of Transylvania, its great oak posts carved with suns, tulips, the tree of life and heraldic symbols. A marriage gate stands before the house and a small gate for the dead leads to the yard, making each carving a family record.
source: Hungarian and Székely ethnography of folk architecture

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the embroidered shepherd's coat of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length wool felt cloak covered with appliquéd floral and rosette patterns in coloured wool. Worn by herdsmen and hung as a sign of rank, its rich surface made it a prized gift and heirloom.
material: white wool felt, coloured wool thread
source: Hungarian folk costume studies

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary is the golden coronation crown of Saint Stephen I, decorated with cloisonné enamel plaques and a bent cross. Kept in the Hungarian Parliament in Budapest, it symbolises Hungarian statehood and was used to crown kings until 1916, though its age and true origin remain debated.
aliases: Crown of Saint Stephen of Hungary
source: Academic studies of the Hungarian coronation insignia

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is a Bulgarian talisman of twisted red and white yarn, with a small pendant, given on 1 March to wish health and spring. Worn on the wrist until a stork or blossom appears, it honours Baba Marta, and the shared custom is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
source: Bulgarian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are Bulgarian winter ritual figures, men dressed in sheepskin costumes with tall carved wooden masks, animal hides and heavy bronze bells who dance through villages at New Year and before Lent to drive away evil spirits and bring fertility. The rite is strongest in the Pernik and Shoppe regions.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, a goatskin bag with a chanter and drone, played at weddings, festivals and shepherds' pastures. Its bright, reedy voice leads horo dances, and it is considered the most beloved national instrument of Bulgarian folk music.
source: Bulgarian ethnomusicology

name: Mărțișor
description: Mărțișorul is the Romanian March talisman, a red-and-white silk thread tied with a small charm or coin, offered on 1 March for health and good luck. Worn through the month and then hung on a fruit tree, it welcomes spring, and is shared in the UNESCO-inscribed 1 March customs.
material: red and white silk thread, metal charm or coin
source: Romanian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Troiță
description: Troița is the Romanian wayside cross, a hand-carved oak cross sheltered by a small roof, placed at roadsides, springs and crossroads to guard travellers and honour the dead. Maramureș carvers cover them with vines and geometric rosettes, making each troiță a prayer in wood.
source: Romanian ethnography of folk architecture and religion

name: Dacian Gold Bracelets
description: The Dacian gold bracelets are spiral gold arm rings from the kingdom of Dacia, cast in the mid-1st century BC and buried at Sarmizegetusa Regia. Looted in 2000 and partly recovered, they now belong to the Historical Treasury of the National History Museum in Bucharest and are masterpieces of Dacian goldwork.
source: Archaeological studies of the Sarmizegetusa Regia treasure

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the Serbian cap with a raised V-shaped crown, descended from the cloth caps of the 18th-century šajkaši river troops who patrolled the Danube. Worn by Serbian soldiers and peasants, and in the Serbian military tradition, it became a national headgear symbol.
source: Histories of Serbian military dress and ethnography

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, made on a vertical loom with geometric medallions and borders in red, black, green and white. Woven for centuries for floors, walls and weddings, it is counted a national symbol of Serbian weaving.
source: Serbian textile and craft studies

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is traditional Serbian peasant footwear, a soft leather moccasin with a turned-up pointed toe and leather straps, hand-made and waterproof. Its curling toe, worn for walking in grass and hills, made it a marker of Serbian village identity and folk dress.
source: Serbian folk dress studies

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, formed by layering fish-scale essence over a mother-of-pearl core, made in Ohrid workshops for about a century. Their warm lustre and entirely manual method made them a signature craft of Ohrid and the region's jewellers.
source: Macedonian craft and jewellery studies

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a North Macedonian double flute, two parallel pipes carved from one piece of wood or bone with fingerholes on one pipe, played by shepherds. Its paired pipes sound a drone with the melody, and it accompanies Macedonian pastoral and festive music.
source: Macedonian ethnomusicology

name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: Woolen coat of Georgian men with a fitted waist, flared skirt and rows of decorative cartridge loops (gazyr) across the chest. Worn since at least the 17th century across the Caucasus, the chokha remains the emblem of Georgian national dress and is now reserved mostly for festivals, dance and ceremony.
source: Georgian National Museum, Tbilisi; ethnographic dress studies of the Caucasus

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: Drinking vessel of the Georgian highlands carved from the curved horn of an ox or mountain goat, sometimes mounted in chased silver, and used for wine at feasts. Raised during the traditional Georgian toast, the kantsi is especially associated with Svaneti and Khevsureti feast custom; the largest examples rest on a stand or are passed from hand to hand around the table of drinking companions.
material: ox or goat horn, chased silver (festive examples)
source: Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Georgian feast (supra) custom studies

name: Panduri (Georgian Three-String Lute)
description: Three-stringed fretted lute of Georgia with a shallow wooden body and gut or nylon strings, played to accompany songs and instrumental pieces. Traditionally hung on the wall of the house when not in use, the panduri accompanies both men's and women's singing; with the larger four-string chonguri it is the most common plucked instrument of Georgian folk music and an emblem of Georgian tradition.
material: mulberry or other wood, gut/nylon strings
source: Georgian folk music tradition; hangebi.ge folk instrument documentation

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: Four-stringed fretless lute of western Georgia carved from a single block of walnut or maple, with a shallow bowl body and a shorter drone string called zili. Associated with the Megrel and Gurian lowlands, the chonguri traditionally accompanied women's songs and the evening work gatherings (nadi); its strings are named after the voices of Georgian polyphonic song.
material: walnut or maple, spruce soundboard, nylon strings
source: Smithsonian 'Georgian Chonguri' object of the day; Georgian folk instrument studies (Arakishvili)

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: Three-string bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, with a circular or tubular body and a skin soundboard, played to accompany songs and dances. Because bowed strings sustain long notes, the chuniri (and its two-string cousin the chianuri) can stand in for a singing voice in Svan hunting songs and choral music; it is one of the two traditional bowed instruments of Georgia.
material: wood body, skin soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Wikipedia 'Chuniri'; Georgian folk music instrument documentation

name: Qvevri (Georgian Wine Vessel)
description: Large egg-shaped earthenware vessel used to make and age Georgian wine, buried up to the neck in the cellar floor with only the rim above ground. Grapes, must and skins ferment and rest in the qvevri for months, giving the wine its tannic, amber character; the method is at least 8,000 years old, and UNESCO inscribed ancient Georgian qvevri wine-making in 2013.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method' (2013)

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: Freestanding stele of Armenia carved from a single slab of local stone, usually tuff, with an ornamented cross set over a rosette or wheel of eternity and covered in interlace, vine and pomegranate motifs. Erected from the 9th century as tombstones, memorials and church stones, khachkars link the secular and the divine; in 2010 UNESCO inscribed their art on its intangible heritage list.
material: volcanic tuff or other local stone
source: UNESCO ICH 'Armenian cross-stones art. Symbolism and craftsmanship of Khachkars' (2010)

name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
description: Double-reed woodwind of Armenia made from apricot wood, with a wide interchangeable reed, played with circular breathing to produce a warm, vocal tone. The duduk accompanies song, dance and lament and is central to Armenian instrumental tradition; its music was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2008.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Duduk and its music' (2008)

name: Tar (Azerbaijani Long-Necked Lute)
description: Long-necked plucked lute of Azerbaijan with a figure-of-eight wooden body, a lambskin soundboard and six steel strings, held diagonally and plucked with a plectrum. The tar leads the mugham trio and accompanies ashiq song; its craftsmanship and performance art were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2012. It is one of the few national instruments for which Azerbaijani composers wrote concert works.
material: mulberry wood, lambskin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar' (2012)

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: Bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, with a spherical wooden body covered in fish- or lambskin, a long neck and four steel strings, played upright with the bow. Alongside the tar it leads the mugham trio and folk ensembles; the art of crafting and playing the kamancha was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2017. Its small, bright tone carries well in indoor ensembles.
material: walnut or mulberry wood, skin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Art of crafting and playing with kamancha' (2017)

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: Square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, dyed and decorated with woodblock-printed border ornaments, most often the buta (teardrop) motif, with white, red and dark colours marking age and occasion. Woven mainly in Sheki and the Basgal settlement, the kelaghayi is worn at weddings, mourning and daily life; its making and symbolism were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014.
era: silk tradition from c. 7th century; kelaghayi to present
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art and symbolism of Kelaghayi' (2014)

name: Shebeke (Sheki Stained-Glass Lattice)
description: Stained-glass window of Sheki, Azerbaijan, made by fitting hundreds of small pieces of coloured glass into a lattice of walnut strips that interlock without glue or nails. The finest example survives in the 1762 Sheki Khan's Palace, whose roughly 190 windows hold up to 5,000 fragments of glass; masters call the craft 'the art of patience', as a single panel can take months.
source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace' (2019); Art of Shebeke (national ICH inventory)

name: Shahmaran Amulet
description: Amulet bearing the image of Shahmaran, the serpent queen of Caucasian and Anatolian legend, a figure with a woman's head and a serpent body, worn or hung for protection against the evil eye. Amulets, jewellery and wall paintings of the serpent queen are attested across centuries, and her image survives in major collections such as the British Museum and in Azerbaijani amulets and carpet motifs.
material: silver or brass, engraved or painted serpent-queen image
source: British Museum collection (E AF.77); Shahmaran legend of Azerbaijan and Anatolia

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Copper and brass vessels of the Lahij craft town of Azerbaijan, including ewers, basins, cauldrons and trays hammered from a single sheet of metal and engraved with geometric and floral patterns, often coated with a silvery tin alloy. Copper craftsmanship of Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2015; the trade flourished in the 19th century, when Lahij copperware was sold along the Silk Road.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Copper craftsmanship of Lahij' (2015)

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: Handwoven knotted carpet of Azerbaijan, whose regional schools include Caucasian, Tabriz, Karabakh, Shirvan and Baku weaving, with distinctive motifs such as the buta, dragon and stylised garden. Carpet weaving is a women's craft passed down in families; the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2010, and carpets remain the country's best-known craft.
material: wool pile, cotton warp, natural dyes
era: attested from the Middle Ages; classical schools 16th-19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving' (2010)

name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest on an island oak; the hero must break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore.
material: iron needle (in the tale, nested in egg, duck, hare, chest)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Koschei the Deathless)

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Baba Yaga tales)

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('The Firebird')

name: Vasilisa's Doll
description: Small wooden doll given to Vasilisa by her dying mother in the Russian fairy tale, which eats a morsel of the girl's food and helps her perform impossible tasks so that she survives her cruel stepmother and Baba Yaga. Recorded in Afanasyev's collection as 'Vasilisa the Beautiful', the doll is the helper-object of the tale, a folk counterpart to the magical helpers of later European fairy tales.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('Vasilisa the Beautiful')

name: Gusli (Russian Psaltery)
description: Ancient Russian plucked zither, a shallow trapezoid or helmet-shaped board with gut or metal strings, played by the epic singers who performed the byliny. The legendary Novgorod merchant Sadko of the byliny plays the gusli so well that the Sea Tsar summons him to the underwater palace; the instrument is attested in chronicles, miniatures and archaeological finds from Novgorod.
source: Novgorod archaeological finds; byliny of Sadko

name: Samovar (Russian Tea Urn)
description: Metal urn with a central fire-tube used to boil water for tea, a fixture of the Russian home from the early 18th century. The great workshops at Tula and in Moscow produced brass, nickel and silver samovars; around the samovar the family gathered for the evening tea, and it became a byword for hospitality in Russian daily life and literature.
source: Tula State Museum of Samovars; Russian Museum of Decorative Arts

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making.
era: attested from the 17th century; standardised late 19th century
source: Russian folk music tradition; Andreyev's balalaika orchestra (1888)

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces.
material: brocade, velvet, silk, pearls, gold thread
source: Russian Ethnographic Museum; historic Russian dress studies

name: Rushnyk (Ukrainian Ritual Cloth)
description: Embroidered ritual cloth of Ukraine woven from linen or hemp and decorated with geometric and floral embroidery at both ends. The rushnyk hangs on icons, frames doors and windows, joins the couple's hands at weddings and lines the coffin at funerals; its patterns carry protective meaning, and a woman's rushnyk collection testified to her skill.
source: Ivan Honchar Museum; Ukrainian ethnographic collections

name: Pysanka (Ukrainian Decorated Egg)
description: Ukrainian Easter egg decorated by the wax-resist method: a stylus called pysachok draws lines of hot beeswax on the shell, which is then dyed in successive colours, ending with the wax melted away to reveal the pattern. Pysanky bear solar, plant and animal motifs linked to spring rebirth, and eggs were kept in the house as protective charms.
source: Ukrainian pysanka tradition; Lviv Ethnography Museum collections

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century.
material: wood body, gut or metal strings
era: attested from at least the 18th century
source: Ukrainian bandura tradition; studies of the dumy epics

name: Slutsk Belt
description: Woven silk belt produced from the mid-18th century at the Slutsk manufactory of the Radziwiłł family in present-day Belarus, worn with the kontusz coat by Polish-Lithuanian nobility. Double-sided silk with gold and silver thread, floral and checkered borders and maker's marks woven into the ends; genuine Slutsk belts were prized across the Commonwealth and are now a national symbol of Belarus.
maker: Slutsk manufactory, founded by Michał Kazimierz Radziwiłł
source: National Museum of Belarus, Slutsk belt collection

name: Latvian Josta (Woven Belt)
description: Ornamental belt woven by Latvian women on a small rigid loom, patterned with geometric symbols of the sun, moon and stars and the zigzag josta motif, worn by men to hold shirt and breeches. A full-length josta measures several metres and is wound twice around the waist; its weaving is a living craft, and the Latvian National Centre for Culture keeps a register of master weavers.
source: Latvian National Centre for Culture (josta pattern register)

name: Romanian Blouse (Ie)
description: Traditional Romanian blouse, the ie, a linen or cotton chemise whose sleeves and shoulders carry dense geometric embroidery; the shoulder ornament, altița, marks the wearer's region and status. Worn in village dress through the 20th century, the ie entered art and fashion through painters such as Matisse; in 2022 UNESCO inscribed 'the traditional blouse with altița'.
material: linen or cotton, cotton or silk thread
source: UNESCO ICH 'The traditional blouse with altița' (2022, Romania)

name: Cimbalom (Hungarian Hammered Dulcimer)
description: Large hammered dulcimer of Hungary, a trapezoid box with rows of metal strings struck by small wooden hammers; the concert cimbalom developed in Budapest in the 1870s. It appears in Romani music and in the works of composers such as Kodály and Bartók, while its village relatives are played across Eastern Europe; the Hungarian word cimbalom names the whole family of hammered dulcimers.
material: wood box, metal strings, wooden hammers
era: concert form from the 1870s; village instruments older
source: Hungarian cimbalom tradition; Kodály and Bartók repertoire

name: Polish Pisanki (Decorated Eggs)
description: Polish Easter eggs decorated by several regional techniques: batik wax-resist (pisanki), scratch-carving, and the solid raspberry-dyed eggs called byki. Patterns of rays, stars and plant sprigs vary by region, with Kraków, Łowicz and the Opoczno district known for distinct styles; eggs were exchanged at Easter as gifts and kept in the home as charms.
material: hen's egg, beeswax, dyes, scratching tools
source: National Ethnographic Museum, Warsaw; Polish ethnographic collections

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture.
material: steel blade, ash or beech haft
source: Podhale highland culture studies; Tatra Museum, Zakopane

name: Dombra (Kazakh Two-String Lute)
description: Pear-shaped, long-necked two-stringed plucked lute of the Kazakh steppe, the country's signature instrument. Solo instrumental pieces (kuy) performed on dombra are central to Kazakh identity and the tradition of Dombra Kuy is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. Legendary kuishi like Qurmangazy composed famous kuys on it, and epic singers accompanied their tales with the instrument.
material: wood (often apricot or pine), gut/nylon strings
era: ancient; kuy tradition documented from 19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Kazakh traditional art of Dombra Kuy' (2014); Kazakh National Museum

name: Qobyz (Kazakh Horsehair Fiddle)
description: Bowed two-string fiddle of shamans and bakhsy among the Kazakhs, carved from a single piece of wood with horsehair strings and a leather-covered resonator. Legend names Korkyt Ata as its inventor; its sound was held to drive away evil spirits, sickness and death. The qobyz remains the emblematic instrument of Kazakh epic and ritual tradition.
material: single block of wood (often apricot), horsehair strings, leather soundboard
source: Korkyt legends of the Book of Dede Korkut cycle; Qazaqstan heritage portal 'Kobyz and Korkut'; ar.culture.ru collections

name: Shanyrak (Yurt Crown)
description: The crown of the Kazakh yurt: a circular wooden rim with radiating cross-beams (uyk) that supports the roof and lets smoke and daylight pass through the top opening. Beyond architecture, the shanyrak is the foremost Kazakh symbol of home, family continuity and the nation; it stands at the centre of Kazakhstan's state emblem, and custom passes the family shanyrak to the household heir.
source: Akorda — National Emblem of Kazakhstan; ar.culture.ru 'Yurt'

name: Saukele (Kazakh Bridal Headdress)
description: Tall conical wedding headdress of Kazakh brides, covered with silver plaques, coral, beads and gemstones, with a fur-trimmed brow and long veils. The most expensive item of a bride's dowry after the yurt, the saukele symbolised the beginning of married life; it was handed down from mother to daughter and worn until the birth of the first child.
material: velvet or cloth, silver plaques, coral, beads, gold thread, fur
source: Omsk Museum of History and Regional Studies; ar.culture.ru 'Saukele'

name: Kamcha (Kazakh Whip)
description: Braided leather whip of the Kazakhs, carried by horsemen and elders as a riding tool and badge of authority. In Kazakh folklore the kamcha carried protective power: the whip of a respected man was hung near a woman in childbirth, and its crack was said to drive off evil spirits. Skilled craftsmen braid the lash from several plaited leather cords.
material: braided leather, wood or bone handle
source: e-history.kz 'The role of the horse in Kazakh culture' (2016); Kazinform feature on whip-braiding

name: Tubeteika (Tatar Skullcap)
description: Hemispherical embroidered skullcap, the traditional headwear of Tatar men. Decorated with silk or velvet embroidery in floral and geometric patterns, the tubeteika was worn at home and in public, while the taller cone-shaped kelepush was worn outdoors. Embroidered tubeteikas were part of festive dress and remain a symbol of Tatar national identity.
source: National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan; tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'

name: Kalfak (Tatar Women's Embroidered Cap)
description: Velvet cap worn by Tatar women, richly embroidered with gold thread, pearls and gilt coins, with a long embroidered tail or tassel hanging down the back. Part of a woman's dowry, the kalfak was the most original piece of Tatar women's festive headwear and demanded great skill in gold embroidery; unlike the man's tubeteika it marked marital status and rank.
material: velvet, gold thread, pearls, gilt coins
source: tatarstan.ru 'Clothes and trappings'; National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Kumgan (Tatar Copper Ewer)
description: Narrow-necked copper or brass ewer with a spout and handle used by the Tatars for water and for the ritual ablution before Muslim prayer. Made by Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), the kumgan was a symbol of the Tatar home, kept with a towelled basin and used at festivals and religious observances. Kazan and the villages of Zakazanye produced the finest examples.
maker: Tatar coppersmiths (bakyrche), Kazan and Zakazanye workshops
source: ar.culture.ru 'Kumgan' (Tatarstan museums); National Museum of the Republic of Tatarstan

name: Khomus (Yakut Jew's Harp)
description: Metal Jew's harp of the Yakut (Sakha) people, an elongated iron frame with a flexible steel tongue, played by plucking the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The khomus imitates bird calls and natural sounds, accompanied songs and held shamanic associations. Yakutsk's Khomus Museum, the republic's Khomus Day and an international festival honour it as a symbol of Sakha culture.
material: iron or steel frame and tongue
source: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Khomus'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Khomus Museum, Yakutsk

name: Serge (Yakut Carved Hitching Post)
description: Carved wooden hitching post of the Yakut (Sakha) people, set up at home and at the ysyakh summer festival, often topped with carved horse-heads. The sacred Aar Baah Serge of the festival stands on the eastern side as a symbolic world-tree, a ladder linking earth to the upper world where the aiyy deities dwell; horses are tied facing east during the celebration.
source: Gogolev et al., 'Yakut National Holiday — Ysyakh: traditions and modernity' (Berghahn Books)

name: Bychakh (Yakut Knife)
description: Traditional knife of the Yakut (Sakha) people, with an asymmetric blade bearing a fuller on one side and a convex edge on the other, a birch-burl handle and a leather sheath. Forged by Yakut blacksmiths from local iron since pre-Russian times, it is used for carving wood, dressing hides and preparing fish and meat — an everyday tool with a remarkably constant design.
material: locally smelted iron, birch burl handle, leather sheath
era: ancient; similar knives found in Yakut burial grounds
source: Wikipedia 'Yakutian knife'; ar.culture.ru 'Yakutian knife'; Russian Museum of Ethnography

name: Choron (Yakut Kumys Vessel)
description: Carved wooden drinking vessel of the Yakut (Sakha) people, made from a single piece of birch or spruce burl, with a conical or rounded body and short legs. The choron is the principal ritual vessel of the ysyakh summer festival, filled with kumys and offered in honour of the aiyy deities, then shared among the celebrants; its elegant form is held to resemble a bird.
source: Gogolev et al., 'Ysyakh' (Berghahn Books); ar.culture.ru 'Choron'

name: Buryat Shaman's Drum (Hese)
description: Oval single-headed frame drum of the Buryat shaman (bo), fitted with a cross-shaped handle and a rawhide head often painted with images of animals and the world tree. Struck to summon spirits and to carry the shaman between the worlds, the drum (hese) is the central instrument of Buryat ritual practice; obtaining one marked the shaman's consecration.
material: wooden frame, rawhide head, iron handle
source: Wierucka, 'Shamanism in the Baikal Region' (2013); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat drum'

name: Buryat Shaman's Horse-Staff
description: Ritual staff of the Buryat shaman, carved from birch wood and topped with a horse's head; senior shamans who had passed the fifth consecration carried iron-tipped versions. In Buryat belief the horse-staff served as the shaman's mount to ride through the spirit world, and it remains a recognised emblem of Buryat shamanic practice alongside the drum.
source: Czaplicka, 'Shamanism in Siberia' (1914); ar.culture.ru 'Buryat shaman's staff'

name: Igil (Tuvan Horsehead Fiddle)
description: Two-stringed bowed fiddle of the Tuvans, its hollow wooden body covered with hide and its neck crowned with a carved horse's head. The igil accompanies khoomei throat singing and Tuvan epic song, evoking the gait and voice of a steppe horse; it is prized across Central Asia and appears in the collection of the Russian Museum of Ethnography.
material: wooden body, hide soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Alash Ensemble; ar.culture.ru 'Igil'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Doshpuluur (Tuvan Three-String Lute)
description: Long-necked, three-stringed plucked lute of the Tuvans, with a small wooden body often carved in a canoe shape and gut or nylon strings. The doshpuluur forms a key part of Tuvan music, accompanying songs and dance and often played in duet with the igil; it is a close relative of the Altai topshur and Mongolian tovshuur.
source: Wikipedia 'Doshpuluur'; ar.culture.ru collections

name: Topshur (Altai Two-String Lute)
description: Two-stringed plucked lute of the Altai people, carved with a shallow bowl body, hide soundboard and gut or horsehair strings. The topshur accompanies the kaychi storytellers, who perform the great Altai heroic epics such as the Tale of Maadai-Kara; its music is bound to Altai oral tradition and is often played before the fire and during ritual.
material: wood body, hide soundboard, gut/horsehair strings
source: ar.culture.ru 'Topshur'; Altai kaychi tradition

name: Altai Komus (Jew's Harp)
description: Jew's harp of the Altai people, usually of metal or wood with a flexible tongue, played by strumming the tongue while holding the frame to the teeth. The komus is widely used for personal music and to accompany songs; its voice imitates natural sounds. It belongs to the same family of Siberian mouth harps as the Yakut khomus and Buryat khuur.
material: iron, brass or wood; steel tongue
source: ar.culture.ru 'Komus (Altai)'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Malitsa (Nenets Reindeer-Fur Coat)
description: Men's winter coat of the Nenets reindeer herders, sewn from reindeer skins with the fur turned inward, a hood attached inside, and worn with a belt (sok) and fur mittens. Decorated with white or red fur tufting and fur mosaic, the malitsa is made from autumn- and winter-killed reindeer and is the herders' everyday Arctic dress.
source: NAO24 official Nenets Autonomous Okrug portal; ar.culture.ru Arctic collections

name: Yaranga (Chukchi Portable Dwelling)
description: Large hemispherical tent dwelling of the coastal Chukchi, built on a wooden frame of poles and whale ribs and covered with walrus skins, with reindeer hides laid inside against the cold. A family camp could stretch up to twenty metres; inside, fur-lined sleeping chambers formed separate rooms. The yaranga was central to Chukchi coastal life.
material: wooden poles, whale ribs, walrus skins, reindeer hides
source: ar.culture.ru 'Chukchi' (Russian Museum of Ethnography collections)

name: Chukchi Walrus-Ivory Carving
description: Carved objects of the Chukchi and Siberian Yupik of the Chukotka coast, worked from walrus tusks into harpoon heads, amulets, figurines and engraved scenes of sea-hunting and animal life. Walrus ivory carving is a hallmark of Chukchi art, celebrated by the Uelen bone-carving workshop and collected by the Russian Museum of Ethnography.
maker: Chukchi and Siberian Yupik carvers, including the Uelen workshop
source: Wikipedia 'Walrus ivory carving'; ar.culture.ru Chukotka collections

name: Evenki Shaman's Costume
description: Ceremonial cloak of the Evenki shaman, sewn from reindeer hide and hung with iron pendants shaped as birds, fish, deer, snakes and human figures that represent the shaman's spirit-helpers, with a fringed apron and iron rattles. The costume is preserved in the collections of the Russian Museum of Ethnography and Siberian regional museums.
material: reindeer hide (rovduga), iron pendants, leather fringe
source: ar.culture.ru 'Evenk shaman costume'; Russian Museum of Ethnography collections

name: Nivkh Shaman's Drum
description: Oval frame drum of the Nivkh people of Sakhalin and the Amur region, with a wooden handle, used by the shaman to accompany spirit journeys and healing rituals. Its sound marks the shaman's passage between the worlds, as recorded by ethnographers including Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney in her study of Nivkh shamanism.
material: wooden frame, hide head, wooden handle
source: Ohnuki-Tierney, 'Nivkh Shamanism' (1981); ar.culture.ru 'Nivkh drum'
